def: A directory plus a SKILL.md file: a reusable package of workflow instructions that tells Claude how to do one specific task.
pitfall: Assuming a Skill is a piece of code or a script. It's Markdown instructions written for Claude to read, not an executable program.
distractor_rationale: Beginners conflate a Skill with a function or script from traditional programming because both 'package reusable logic,' but a Skill is natural-language instruction, not code.

def: The core file of a Skill, containing two parts: YAML frontmatter (metadata) and Markdown instructions (the directions Claude follows).
pitfall: Writing only the frontmatter or only the instructions, so Claude can't recognize or run the Skill correctly.
distractor_rationale: Newcomers forget SKILL.md must contain both parts, because other Markdown files usually have only body text and no frontmatter.

def: The metadata block at the top of SKILL.md, wrapped in triple-dash (---) markers, holding fields like name and description.
pitfall: Forgetting the closing ---, or using wrong indentation inside the frontmatter, so the YAML fails to parse.
distractor_rationale: YAML is strict about indentation and format, but people used to JSON's flexibility often produce malformed frontmatter.

def: A required frontmatter field that defines the Skill's unique identifier; it becomes the command and must use lowercase letters, digits, and hyphens.
pitfall: Using spaces, capital letters, or camelCase in name (like taskOrganizer), so the Skill can't be invoked correctly.
distractor_rationale: People used to filenames or variable names reach for underscores or camelCase, but a Skill name only allows lowercase and hyphens.

def: A required frontmatter field that tells Claude what the Skill does and when to use it. It is the sole basis for automatic triggering.
pitfall: Writing a vague description like 'Helps with tasks,' so Claude never knows when it applies and never loads it on its own.
distractor_rationale: Newcomers treat description as marketing copy for humans, not realizing it's the field Claude matches against to decide whether to load the Skill.

def: When what the user says matches a Skill's description, Claude loads and runs that Skill on its own, with no manual command.
pitfall: Expecting Claude to trigger on 'intent' when the description contains none of the words the user actually says, so the match never fires.
distractor_rationale: Users assume Claude infers synonyms or context, but automatic triggering leans mostly on keyword matching against the description.

def: Calling a Skill directly with /skill-name, which forces Claude to load it without relying on the description matching.
pitfall: Forgetting that the Skill name can't contain spaces or capitals, and typing /MySkill or /my skill so the call fails.
distractor_rationale: People used to command lines separate arguments with spaces, but a Skill name itself can't contain spaces.

def: Everything in SKILL.md after the frontmatter: the concrete, step-by-step directions Claude follows, written in Markdown.
pitfall: Writing vague steps like 'analyze the data' or 'process the task,' so Claude has no idea what to actually do and the output misses.
distractor_rationale: People used to writing high-level abstractions overlook that Claude needs very specific steps, because it won't 'get what you mean' the way a person would.

def: Giving Claude only what it needs right now instead of dumping every detail at once, so the Skill stays short and loads fast.
pitfall: Trying to cover every edge case in version one and producing a 500-line SKILL.md that loads slowly and is hard to maintain.
distractor_rationale: Perfectionists write too much in the first pass, not knowing progressive disclosure is core to Skill design: concise beats comprehensive.

def: Files in a Skill directory other than SKILL.md (checklists, config, scripts) that are loaded on demand and don't consume initial context.
pitfall: Cramming every check rule into SKILL.md, making the file huge and burning context on every load.
distractor_rationale: People unaware supporting files exist assume everything must live in SKILL.md, missing the benefit of modular organization.

def: Skills stored in ~/.claude/skills/, available only to you but usable across every project. Good for personal habits and general-purpose tools.
pitfall: Putting a team-standard Skill in personal skills, so teammates can't use it.
distractor_rationale: People who don't know the personal-vs-project distinction assume every Skill belongs in ~/.claude/skills/.

def: Skills stored in a project's .claude/skills/ directory, committed to Git so teammates get them automatically when they clone the repo.
pitfall: Adding project skills to .gitignore, so teammates can't sync them and the point of sharing is lost.
distractor_rationale: People habitually ignore dot-directories as local config, not knowing .claude/skills/ is meant to be committed to version control.

def: One of the three traits that make a scenario suit a Skill: you do the same thing daily, weekly, sometimes hourly.
pitfall: Creating a Skill for a one-off task, then never using it again after writing it.
distractor_rationale: People overestimate how often a task repeats, or confuse a varying process with varying content; only a repeating process suits a Skill.

def: One of the three traits that make a scenario suit a Skill: the process can be written as clear steps rather than changing every time.
pitfall: Building a Skill for fully open-ended creative work, which then needs heavy manual intervention on every run.
distractor_rationale: People assume a Skill can handle any task, not knowing it fits structured, repeatable workflows far better than open-ended ones.

def: One of the three traits that make a scenario suit a Skill: you can tell whether Claude got the result right.
pitfall: Building a Skill for a subjective judgment call (like 'is this design any good'), where you can't verify the output quality.
distractor_rationale: People expect a Skill to handle tasks needing taste or business judgment, but those have no objective standard to write into a checklist.

def: The guideline for writing an effective description: what it does + when to use it + key capabilities.
pitfall: Writing only 'what it does' and dropping 'when to use it,' so Claude has no signal for which scenario to load it in.
distractor_rationale: People assume a shorter description is better, not realizing that leaving out the use case breaks automatic triggering.

def: The words in a description that a user might plausibly say; Claude matches on these to decide whether to auto-load the Skill.
pitfall: Writing 'generate documentation' in the description while the user says 'create docs' or 'write docs,' so the keywords don't match and it never fires.
distractor_rationale: People assume Claude understands synonyms, not knowing you should write the various phrasings a user might use into the description.

def: The instructions section that spells out what kind of input the Skill accepts, including shape, source, and a concrete example.
pitfall: Never stating the input format, so Claude can't handle input that arrives in an unexpected shape.
distractor_rationale: People assume Claude auto-detects any format, not knowing that stating the input format explicitly sharply improves accuracy.

def: The ordered, concrete operations the Skill runs; the heart of the instructions, where each step should be specific enough to be unambiguous.
pitfall: Writing vague steps like 'analyze the input' or 'judge priority' with no stated criteria, so Claude doesn't know the actual standard to apply.
distractor_rationale: People used to writing high-level flow overlook that Claude needs explicit decision criteria, like 'contains "urgent" -> Urgent.'

def: The instructions section defining what the result should look like, including structure, symbols, and a worked example.
pitfall: Saying only 'output a list' with no example, so Claude's output format comes out different on every run.
distractor_rationale: People assume Claude knows what a 'standard format' is, not knowing a complete example is what guarantees consistent formatting.

def: Unusual or abnormal inputs (empty input, malformed input, over-long content) whose handling must be spelled out explicitly in the instructions.
pitfall: Testing only well-behaved input, so the Skill misbehaves or stalls on an empty string or garbled format.
distractor_rationale: People focus on the happy path and skip edge cases, not knowing that's the main reason a Skill turns out unstable.

def: The simplest test: call the Skill with /skill-name and watch whether the output matches expectations.
pitfall: Testing once, seeing it work, and declaring the Skill fine, without preparing multiple cases across different situations.
distractor_rationale: People underestimate the variability of AI behavior; one success doesn't mean every run succeeds, and several cases are needed to prove stability.

def: Prepared input-and-expected-output pairs used to test a Skill systematically before relying on it.
pitfall: Preparing only normal-case tests and never covering edge or garbage input.
distractor_rationale: Incomplete testing mindset: people don't realize edge and abnormal cases are where the real problems surface.

def: The test-find-fix-retest cycle a Skill goes through; the path from 'it runs' to 'it runs well.'
pitfall: Expecting version one to be perfect and giving up at the first problem, not knowing every good Skill is iterated into shape.
distractor_rationale: Perfectionists won't accept a flawed first version, so they miss the chance to learn and improve from real use.

def: Running the same task with and without the Skill and timing both, to prove whether the Skill is actually faster and more consistent.
pitfall: Assuming a Skill saves time just because it exists, without measuring, then finding the Skill version is slower or lower quality.
distractor_rationale: People let subjective impression stand in for objective measurement, not knowing you need data to confirm a Skill's real value.

def: Organizing a complex task as a series of explicit check items, each of which can independently pass or fail.
pitfall: Writing check items too vaguely (like 'check code quality'), so there's no clear way to judge pass or fail.
distractor_rationale: People miss that the point of a checklist is measurability: every item needs an explicit pass/fail standard.

def: A Skill that runs several sequential steps to finish a complex task, where one step's output may feed the next.
pitfall: Leaving the dependencies between steps unclear, so Claude runs them out of order or skips an intermediate step.
distractor_rationale: People assume Claude infers step dependencies, not knowing you must write 'step 2 uses the result of step 1' explicitly.

def: Splitting a Skill's findings by severity (passed, worth a look, must fix) so the reader knows what to act on first.
pitfall: Listing every problem flat, so the user can't tell which items must be fixed now and which can wait.
distractor_rationale: People think listing problems is enough, not knowing severity grading is what makes a Skill usable, letting the reader decide fast.

def: Managing project skills with Git so you can view history, roll back, and compare versions, the same way you manage code.
pitfall: Editing a Skill but never committing it, so teammates keep using the old version and the review bar drifts apart.
distractor_rationale: People treat a Skill as a config file to tweak freely, not knowing it also needs version control and team syncing.

def: Reviewing a new or changed Skill the way you review code: check the description, the instructions, and the tests before merging.
pitfall: Merging a teammate's Skill without review, then finding the description is too vague or the instructions are wrong.
distractor_rationale: People think a Skill is just documentation and needs no review, not knowing a poor Skill drags down the whole team's efficiency.

def: A team-wide, agreed-on style for Skill names: hyphens, verb-noun or noun-verb order, two or three words.
pitfall: Everyone using a different style (underscores, camelCase, numeric suffixes), which makes Skills hard to manage and find.
distractor_rationale: People don't notice how much naming convention matters and each name things their own way, producing a mess.

def: Reviewing all Skills once a quarter and deleting or improving the ones that barely get used, so an unused pile doesn't crowd Claude's choices.
pitfall: Creating many Skills but never pruning, so Claude has to search a pile of dead Skills at load time.
distractor_rationale: People focus only on adding new Skills and overlook that deleting dead ones is just as important.

def: After changing an existing Skill, post the change and its impact in the team channel so people don't operate the new Skill on old assumptions.
pitfall: Quietly changing code-review's standards, so teammates still read the results by the old bar and get confused.
distractor_rationale: People think editing one file is no big deal, not knowing a Skill change directly shifts the team's workflow and expectations.

def: Chaining several single-purpose Skills to handle one larger task, or referencing one Skill from inside another.
pitfall: Building one big all-in-one Skill that tries to do everything, which then becomes hard to maintain and reuse.
distractor_rationale: People don't grasp that small, focused Skills composed together beat a monolithic Skill, which violates single responsibility.

def: An optional frontmatter field that restricts a Skill to a specified set of tools, drawing a permission boundary for security-sensitive cases.
pitfall: Leaving tools unrestricted, so the Skill unexpectedly uses a tool it shouldn't (editing files, running scripts).
distractor_rationale: People don't know tool permissions can be limited and assume a Skill just won't do anything dangerous on its own.

def: An optional frontmatter field that, when set, stops Claude from auto-loading the Skill, leaving manual invocation only, to avoid accidental triggers.
pitfall: Building an expensive Skill (one that calls a paid API) without disabling auto-invocation, so it fires by accident and runs up cost.
distractor_rationale: People don't know this field exists and assume the only way to avoid accidental triggers is to edit the description.

def: An optional frontmatter field that pins a specific model for the Skill, for example a stronger reasoning model when the task needs it.
pitfall: Leaving every Skill on the default model, so a Skill that needs careful reasoning comes out inconsistent.
distractor_rationale: People don't know a model can be set per Skill and assume it's a global setting only.

def: A Model Context Protocol server that supplies tools (database access, API calls) to Claude; a Skill supplies the workflow knowledge for using them.
pitfall: Having an MCP tool but not knowing how to use it, or writing a Skill with no matching MCP tool to back it.
distractor_rationale: People confuse MCP (supplies tools) with Skills (supply workflow), missing that the two are complementary.

def: Skills built and shared by other developers, findable on GitHub and elsewhere.
pitfall: Copying a community Skill straight into a production project without first vetting it for safety and fit.
distractor_rationale: People over-trust community resources, not knowing you should first try it in a scratch project and check for anything risky.

def: Listing every project skill, with usage and examples, in the project README or .claude/README.md.
pitfall: Creating many project skills but documenting none, so new members don't know which Skills exist or how to use them.
distractor_rationale: People think the Skill file is its own documentation, not knowing you need an index so people can find and understand what's available.

def: Each Skill should do one thing and do it well, rather than trying to solve several unrelated problems in one Skill.
pitfall: Building an 'everything assistant' Skill that tries to handle every task and ends up doing each one poorly.
distractor_rationale: People chase the convenience of 'one Skill for everything,' not grasping that small, focused Skills are easier to maintain and compose.

def: When Claude loads a Skill, the SKILL.md content occupies the context window; the longer the file, the more it consumes.
pitfall: Writing a 500-line SKILL.md, so every load burns a large amount of context and crowds out Claude's ability to handle other information.
distractor_rationale: People don't realize context is a limited resource and assume more detail is always better.

def: Supporting-file content is read only when Claude actually needs it, so it doesn't occupy context at the Skill's initial load.
pitfall: Writing everything into SKILL.md and never using the on-demand loading that supporting files provide.
distractor_rationale: People don't grasp the technical mechanism behind progressive disclosure and assume splitting files is just about organizing code.

def: When a Skill flags normal code or content as a problem; fix it by adding a 'needs confirmation' category or tuning the criteria.
pitfall: A high false-positive rate forces the user to hand-filter every run, making the Skill slower than not using one.
distractor_rationale: Check rules written too strictly, or that ignore special cases, produce a flood of false positives.

def: When a Skill fails to catch a problem it should have found; fix it by adding check rules or adjusting the judgment logic.
pitfall: A code review Skill misses an obvious gap in error handling, and the user loses trust in it.
distractor_rationale: Check rules aren't comprehensive enough and don't cover common problem scenarios.

def: When a Skill won't auto-load or a manual call fails, the diagnostic process of checking file path, frontmatter format, and name spelling in that order.
pitfall: The Skill file exists but won't invoke, and with no idea where to start, the person changes things blindly and makes it worse.
distractor_rationale: People lack a systematic diagnosis method and try things at random, not knowing to check file path -> frontmatter format -> name spelling in order.

def: Providing input/output examples so Claude understands the expected behavior; a worked example does more than prose description.
pitfall: Describing the format in words only, so Claude misreads it and the output diverges from what you wanted.
distractor_rationale: People think a prose description is already clear, not knowing Claude learns far better from an example than from words.

def: Creating or changing an experimental Skill on a Git branch and merging to main only once it earns it, so the team isn't disrupted.
pitfall: Editing a Skill directly on main, breaking it, and disrupting the whole team's work.
distractor_rationale: People don't know a branch can isolate experimental changes, or worry branch management is too complex.

def: Knowledge about how to organize steps, when to use which tool, and how to judge the result; the core value a Skill supplies.
pitfall: Supplying only the tools (an MCP server) with no workflow knowledge, so Claude doesn't know how to use them to finish the task.
distractor_rationale: People assume having the tools is enough, not knowing workflow knowledge is the bridge between tools and the goal.
